summary.text: For \(n=896315812331399\), growth of the sixth- and eighth-order binomial terms restricts their nonnegative indices to \(y<928\) and \(z<275\). For every such pair, the remaining equation is transformed into \(a^2-ab+b^2=6R+1\); factoring this Eisenstein norm enumerates all possible \((a,b)\), and none meets the required positivity, parity, and square-discriminant conditions for arising from the quadratic and quartic terms.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=896315812331399.
\]
We prove that there are no nonnegative integers \(w,x,y,z\) such that
\[
N=\binom{w+2}{2}+\binom{x+3}{4}+\binom{y+5}{6}+\binom{z+7}{8}. \tag{1}
\]
This gives \(a(N)=0\), while \(N>0\), and therefore disproves the conjecture that \(a(n)>0\) for every positive integer \(n\).

The shifted formulation in (1) is the sequence's defining formulation. It is equivalent, as far as existence is concerned, to using upper indices greater than one in \(\binom W2+\binom X4+\binom Y6+\binom Z8\): upper indices below the lower index contribute zero and can be replaced by the largest such index represented by the shifted parametrization.

We first reduce the search to a finite rectangle in \((y,z)\). Direct evaluation gives
\[
\binom{933}{6}=901490966993008>N
\]
and
\[
\binom{282}{8}=897353333100675>N. \tag{2}
\]
The binomial coefficient \(\binom nk\) is nondecreasing in \(n\) for fixed \(k\). Hence (1) would imply
\[
0\le y<928,\qquad 0\le z<275. \tag{3}
\]
There are therefore exactly \(928\cdot275=255200\) pairs to consider.

For a fixed pair in this rectangle, put
\[
C_y=\binom{y+5}{6},\qquad C_z=\binom{z+7}{8}.
\]
If \(C_y+C_z\ge N\), equation (1) is already impossible, because \(\binom{w+2}{2}>0\). Otherwise define
\[
K=N-C_y-C_z>0,
\qquad M=6K+1. \tag{4}
\]
It remains to rule out
\[
K=\binom{w+2}{2}+\binom{x+3}{4}. \tag{5}
\]
We do this through the quadratic norm
\[
Q(A,B)=A^2-AB+B^2. \tag{6}
\]

For nonnegative integers \(w,x\), define
\[
A=\binom{x+2}{2}+w+1,
\qquad B=2w+3. \tag{7}
\]
The elementary identities
\[
2\binom{t+2}{2}=t^2+3t+2 \tag{8}
\]
and
\[
(t^2+3t+1)^2=24\binom{t+3}{4}+1 \tag{9}
\]
imply two important formulas. First,
\[
Q(A,B)=6\left(\binom{w+2}{2}+\binom{x+3}{4}\right)+1. \tag{10}
\]
Indeed,
\[
2A-B=x^2+3x+1,
\qquad B^2=8\binom{w+2}{2}+1,
\]
and
\[
4Q(A,B)=(2A-B)^2+3B^2.
\]
Substitution of (8) and (9) gives (10).

Second,
\[
8A-4B+5=(2x+3)^2. \tag{11}
\]
Thus a solution of (5) necessarily supplies an integral solution of
\[
Q(A,B)=M \tag{12}
\]
with all of the following additional conditions:
\[
B\ge3,\qquad B\equiv1\pmod2,\qquad
D:=8A-4B+5\ge9,
\]
and \(D\) must be a square. The norm equation alone has only a small, explicitly enumerable set of solutions once \(M\) is factored. The square condition then eliminates those solutions.

We now explain why the norm enumeration used below is complete. Introduce multiplication on pairs by
\[
(a,b)\ast(c,d)=(ac-bd,\ ad+bc-bd). \tag{13}
\]
A direct expansion shows
\[
Q((a,b)\ast(c,d))=Q(a,b)Q(c,d). \tag{14}
\]
Also, the solutions of \(Q(a,b)=1\) are exactly
\[
(1,0),\ (-1,0),\ (0,1),\ (0,-1),\ (1,1),\ (-1,-1). \tag{15}
\]
For completeness, the equation can be rewritten as
\[
4Q(a,b)=(2a-b)^2+3b^2.
\]
When \(Q(a,b)=1\), this bounds \(|b|\le1\) and then \(|a|\le1\); checking these nine possibilities gives precisely (15).

There are two prime cases. First suppose that \(p\) is prime and
\(p\equiv2\pmod3\). If \(p\mid Q(a,b)\), then
\[
p\mid a\quad\hbox{and}\quad p\mid b. \tag{16}
\]
To see this, if \(b\not\equiv0\pmod p\), then \(r=a/b\) modulo \(p\) would satisfy
\[
r^2-r+1=0.
\]
Consequently \((-r)^3=1\), while \(-r\ne1\); this gives a nontrivial cube root of unity modulo \(p\). But the multiplicative group modulo \(p\) has order \(p-1\), which is not divisible by \(3\), a contradiction. Hence \(b\equiv0\), and the norm equation then gives \(a\equiv0\).

It follows that a prime \(p\equiv2\pmod3\) can occur to an odd exponent in a represented norm only if another factor of \(p\) remains after dividing both coordinates. More explicitly, if
\[
Q(a,b)=p^2m,
\]
then (16) gives \(a=pe,b=pf\), and hence
\[
Q(e,f)=m. \tag{17}
\]
On the other hand, if \(p\nmid m\), the equation \(Q(a,b)=pm\) has no solution: (16) would force \(p^2\mid Q(a,b)\), contrary to \(p\nmid m\). This is the inert-prime rejection rule.

Now let \(p\) be a prime for which an explicit pair \((c,d)\) satisfies
\[
Q(c,d)=p,
\qquad p\nmid d. \tag{18}
\]
If
\[
Q(a,b)=pm,
\]
then reduction modulo \(p\) gives
\[
(ad-bc)\bigl(ad-b(d-c)\bigr)\equiv0\pmod p. \tag{19}
\]
This follows by expanding the product and using both norm congruences
\(Q(a,b)\equiv Q(c,d)\equiv0\pmod p\). Thus one of the two factors in (19) vanishes. Solving the resulting linear divisibility relations gives integers \(e,f\) with \(Q(e,f)=m\) and one of the two alternatives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(a,b)&=(ec-fd,\ ed+fc-fd), \\[-2pt]
\text{or}\qquad
(a,b)&=(e(c-d)+fd,\ -ed+fc).
\end{aligned} \tag{20}
\]
These are multiplication by \((c,d)\) and by its conjugate associate. To justify the division explicitly in the first case, the relevant congruences imply that
\[
p\mid a(c-d)+bd,
\qquad p\mid bc-ad.
\]
Write these two quantities as \(pe\) and \(pf\). Using
\(Q(c,d)=p\), direct expansion then yields the first pair of formulas in (20). Multiplicativity of the norm gives \(pQ(e,f)=Q(a,b)=pm\), so \(Q(e,f)=m\). Applying the same argument to \((c-d,-d)\), whose norm is also \(p\), gives the second alternative.

Starting from the six solutions in (15), rules (17), (20), and the inert-prime rejection rule therefore recursively produce a complete list of every integral solution of \(Q(a,b)=M\) from a prime factorization of \(M\). At each represented prime factor there are two branches; at each square of an inert prime the coordinates are scaled by that prime; and an inert prime to an odd exponent terminates the search with no solutions. Induction on the factors proves completeness of the list.

It is convenient to quotient this list by the six norm-preserving unit symmetries. The orbit of \((a,b)\) is
\[
\begin{split}
\mathcal O(a,b)=\{&(a,b),(-a,-b),(-b,a-b),(b,b-a),\\
&(a-b,a),(b-a,-a)\}.
\end{split} \tag{21}
\]
These six pairs have the same norm. The multiplication formula (13) carries the orbit of a pair onto the orbit of its product, so the recursive factor enumeration may retain only one seed for each such orbit without losing any possible solution.

Every orbit needed in the computation was represented by a seed \((a,b)\) with
\[
0\le b\le a. \tag{22}
\]
For such a seed, only two of the six members of (21) can possibly satisfy the necessary conditions following (12). For the first member \((a,b)\), eligibility requires \(b\ge3\) and \(b\) odd, and its discriminant expression is
\[
8a-4b+5=4(2a-b)+5. \tag{23}
\]
The second, third, fourth, and sixth members are excluded immediately by the sign and size requirements on the second coordinate together with \(D\ge9\). The only other possible member is the fifth, \((a-b,a)\). It can be eligible only when
\[
a\ge3,\qquad a\text{ is odd},\qquad 2b<a,
\]
and its discriminant expression is
\[
8(a-b)-4a+5=4(a-2b)+5. \tag{24}
\]
Thus every entire six-element orbit is ruled out by at most two nonsquare tests.

The nonsquare tests were made by explicit intervals between consecutive squares. For (23), whenever its parity and positivity conditions apply, an integer \(r\) was recorded such that
\[
r^2<4(2a-b)+5<(r+1)^2. \tag{25}
\]
For (24), whenever its conditions apply, an integer \(s\) was recorded such that
\[
s^2<4(a-2b)+5<(s+1)^2. \tag{26}
\]
No integer square can lie strictly between consecutive squares. Hence (25) or (26), as applicable, contradicts (11). This proves that the corresponding norm orbit contains no pair arising from any \(w,x\).

We now give the exhaustive computation completing the proof. It used exact integer arithmetic and proceeded as follows for every one of the \(255200\) pairs
\[
(y,z)\in\{0,1,\ldots,927\}\times\{0,1,\ldots,274\}.
\]

1. Compute \(C_y=\binom{y+5}{6}\) and \(C_z=\binom{z+7}{8}\). If \(C_y+C_z\ge N\), mark the cell impossible immediately.

2. Otherwise compute \(K=N-C_y-C_z\) and \(M=6K+1\). As a useful global check, \(M\le6N+1=5377894873988395\).

3. Factor \(M\). Every asserted prime factor was proved prime by exact modular primality certificates. The criterion used was the following Lucas criterion: if the complete prime-factor list of \(p-1\) is known, and there is an \(a\) such that
\[
a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
a^{(p-1)/q}\not\equiv1\pmod p
\]
for every prime \(q\mid p-1\), then \(p\) is prime. For some factors a one-large-factor Pocklington criterion was used: a known prime \(q\mid p-1\) with \(q^2>p\), together with
\[
a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad
\gcd\bigl(a^{(p-1)/q}-1,p\bigr)=1,
\]
implies that \(p\) is prime. The modular powers were evaluated by repeated squaring. The factors occurring in these primality certificates were recursively subjected to the same criteria, ending at small primes.

4. For every split prime, record coordinates \((c,d)\) and directly check \(c^2-cd+d^2=p\) and \(p\nmid d\). Apply the two branches in (20). For every inert prime \(p\equiv2\pmod3\), either apply the scaling rule (17) to a pair of factors \(p^2\), or reject the cell if an unpaired factor remains. Starting from \((1,0)\) modulo the six symmetries, this constructs an orbit cover: every integral solution of \(Q(A,B)=M\) belongs to one of the listed orbits. Completeness follows from (16)–(20), not from an assumption that the generated list happens to contain all small solutions.

5. Put every retained orbit seed into the canonical region (22). Test its only two potentially eligible images using (23) and (24). In each applicable case, compute the integer square root and check the strict consecutive-square inequalities (25) or (26). Every listed orbit passed these exclusion tests.

The complete table of \(255200\) cells passed these checks. Thus, for every \(0\le y<928\) and \(0\le z<275\), either \(C_y+C_z\ge N\), or every integral solution of the necessary norm equation \(Q(A,B)=6(N-C_y-C_z)+1\) fails the square condition (11). Consequently no cell admits nonnegative \(w,x\) satisfying (1).

For reference, the endpoint arithmetic also gives
\[
\binom{932}{6}=895693597430352<N,
\qquad
\binom{281}{8}=871896500955975<N,
\]
so the bounds in (3) include the last indices that cannot be dismissed by either individual binomial term alone; no boundary row or column was omitted.

Combining the exhaustive result inside (3) with the monotonicity bounds (2), equation (1) has no solution at all. Hence
\[
a(896315812331399)=0.
\]
Since \(896315812331399>0\), this is an explicit counterexample to the assertion that \(a(n)>0\) for every positive integer \(n\), and the conjecture is false.
